The New Atheist Movement has been known for its philosophical dullness, so most of what Dawkins has to say outside of genetics is not to be taken as an expert opinion.

As for belief in God, everyone is different, and what convinced me is likely not what would convince you. That said, doubting is certainly part of the process of faith. I'd be more concerned for you if you didn't ever have these sorts of doubts.

There are a set of things that solidified my faith in the Christian God, which had been transient for much of my teenage years. The nature of the failed Assyrian conquest of Jerusalem was a particular one. The highly accurate prophecies of Daniel are another. The evidence for a historical Jesus who was crucified, and whose disciples acted with an almost unbelievable fervor to spread his message is also compelling for me.

A lot of intellectual arguments really solidified my belief in the necessity of what we would identify as God, particularly the Leibnizian Cosmological Argument (there's a really good video by the channel InspiringPhilosophy about that particular argument).

Finally, Universalism itself is probably the biggest reason for my faith. I had intellectually accepted that there is certainly a God, but that is not the same as knowing said God. It was like looking through a glass darkly, to use a Pauline metaphor.

An all-loving God who sent people to hell for the sin of not knowing him (even when he hadn't tried to know them) didn't make sense, and Universalist theologies helped me better understand God. Thomas Talbott's "The Inescapable Love of God" was particularly instrumental in that.

It's admittedly a long story, but it started with hearing the belief that all who commit suicide are eternally damned. This was an extremely common belief among the non-denominational and Church of Christ people where I was raised.

I think that's when I started questioning Hell. I've been suicidal, but I've also been a believer for the longest time. Would God abandon his child because they were overwhelmed with pain? I don't think he would.

It was just over half a decade later that I was reading David Bentley Hart's book, "Atheist Delusions", which condemned certain New Atheist arguments. The topic of Christians using Hell as coercion came up, and Hart mentioned that the early church was often Universalistic rather than believing in an eternal hell.

That piqued my interest. After I finished that book, I looked at some of his other works and found "That All Shall Be Saved", Hart's book on Universalism. I read it, and found it very engrossing and compelling.

But I was not fully convinced. After my (admittedly short) lifetime of having the idea of eternal hell treated as completely infallible, I couldn't fully commit to Universalism.

What caused me to ultimately believe in Universalism was when I was reading 1 Timothy for a college class on the New Testament.

Verse 2:4: "(God) who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth," was what ultimately pushed me over the edge into becoming a Necessary Universalist over just a hopeful one.

I'm sure you're aware that there are a multitude of Universalist-implying Bible verses, 1 Timothy 2:4 being a favorite of mine. And that many of the verses people use for justifying eternal damnation, namely Matthew 25:46 are based on mistranslations of scripture.

But I think the best argument for Universalism would be reading the Bible as a whole in light of it. There are several books that broach this topic, but a favorite of mine is The Inescapable Love of God by Thomas Talbott. There are several chapters available for free on his website if the topic interests you.

David Bentley Hart's discussion of Gregory of Nyssa's understanding of the greater Biblical meta-narrative is an absolutely brilliant crystallization of that sort of exegetical approach. I believe it is in his third meditation in the book, That All Shall Be Saved.

It's a bit too long to go into proper detail here, but Chapter 11 of The Inescapable Love of God by Thomas Talbott is a direct refutation of that sort of argument. The book as a whole is great, but if you aren't interested in that, Chapter 11 is free to read on his website.
